catalog_quote: 8. In the Congo languages the main accent falls on the initial syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables, whether radical or derivative, follow the accented syllable a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult. EX.—Bapàlangàni, they have scattered; but bapàlanganàka, they scattered. (a) When the prefix attached to a stem consists of a nasal only, for the purposes of accent it is regarded as belonging to the syllable to which it is joined. EX.—M̀pati, a sheep; a-m̀be-ti, he beat me = a-m-be-ti. (b) When in a dissyllabic word, a prefix other than the nasal takes the accent, it will be found generally that the vowel of the prefix has combined with, or been dropped before, an initial vowel of the stem. EX.—Miu, eyes = ma-iu; mumbu, nests = ma-umbu; minu, flesh = mi-inu. Note.—There are some apparent exceptions to this rule, as kulu, leg (Kongo), bato, people (Bangi). It is highly probable, however, that these were dissyllabic stems originally; in the Soko language I find ba-ito, people.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked on the page scan (printed p. 4, "B. On Accent", §8) and the scanned layer ( lines 3655-3697). The quoted §8 text, (a), (b) and the Note are on that page word for word; the only differences are diacritics the compiler normalised (the image prints a grave on the m of "M̀pati"/"a-m̀be-ti", and the accent marks on "Bapàlangàni"/"bapàlangànàka" are as the compiler gave them). §8(c) (Kele accent shift) and §9 ("In Swahili the main accent falls on the penult" + Kele Swahili-loan note) are on p. 5 as reported. Identity: p. v (leaf029 image) states "The dialect chosen and called Ngala is spoken by the Boloki who occupy the settlements of Mangala, Monsembi, (and passing over Liboko) Mobeka on…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word accent on the first syllable of the stem (root), whatever prefixes precede it; a weaker secondary accent on the penultimate syllable when three or more syllables follow the stem-initial syllable (i.e. in long derived verb forms). A prefix consisting of a bare nasal is counted with the following stem syllable. Apparent prefix-accented disyllables (kulu, bato) are explained as historically disyllabic stems. The rule is stated for 'the Congo languages' of the handbook collectively (Kongo, Bangi, Lolo, Ngala, Poto, Ngombe, Soko, Kele), Ngala being the Boloki dialect of Monsembe where Stapleton worked 1890-97; Swahili (penult) is explicitly contrasted. Note the same author says tone is outside his scope (p. 140), and Motingea 2002 (p. 293) describes Boloki as a normal two-tone (H/L) language without mentioning stress, so the 1903 'accent' may reflect stem-initial high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult' when more than two syllables follow the accented stem-initial syllable (example bapàlangànàka).
new_statements.exceptions: Nasal-only prefixes count with the stem syllable (Mpati, a-mbe-ti); prefix-accented disyllables like kulu 'leg' (Kongo), bato 'people' (Bangi) treated as fused/contracted old disyllabic stems; (c) in Kele accent shifts to mark a grammatical distinction; Swahili loans in Kele may keep penultimate accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for nouns and (derived) verb forms; stated comparatively for all eight Congo languages of the handbook, not for Boloki in isolation, though Boloki/Ngala was the author's own field language. Old missionary description (1903) predating tonal analysis; the only modern description (Motingea 2002) is tonal and silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Stapleton 1903 calls the variety 'Ngala' and states (p. v) that it is 'spoken by the Boloki who occupy the settlements of Mangala, Monsembi.. Mobeka.. Bolombo, Dibulula and Bokombi', i.e. the Boloki of Monsembe = bolo1262 (ISO bkt); Motingea 2002 confirms 'ngala' of Stapleton = boloki. Not to be confused with the Bangala/Lingala trade language (bang1353) treated in Stapleton's appendix, nor with the Boloki (Iboko/Mabale) of Mankanza. The accent statement is framed for all the handbook's Congo languages jointly.

When more than two syllables.. follow the accented syllable a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult'; a nasal-only prefix counts with the stem syllable for accent; apparent exceptions (kulu, bato) explained as old disyllabic stems. The handbook's 'Ngala' is explicitly 'spoken by the Boloki who occupy the settlements of Mangala, Monsembi.. Mobeka.. Bolombo, Dibulula and Bokombi' (p. v); Stapleton and Weeks founded Monsembe in 1890, so the Ngala/Boloki data are first-hand…
